items.title: Broad access through consistent standards
items.summary_zh: OpenAI 更新了模型或产品能力更新，关键在于模型能力、部署成本、权限控制或开发者工作流的实际变化。
items.summary_en: How OpenAI works with distribution partners to uphold consistent safeguards, support responsible access, and clarify expectations in our Usage Policies.
items.extracted_excerpt: How OpenAI works with distribution partners to uphold consistent safeguards, support responsible access, and clarify expectations in our Usage Policies.
items.extracted_text_for_analysis: Over the past few months, we’ve worked with customers and partners to align safety policies across services that provide our models. We’re also updating our Usage Policies to make those requirements clearer and easier for developers to follow. Models such as GPT‑6 Astra expand what developers and businesses can build. As those capabilities grow, we’re working to keep safeguards effective and consistently applied across the services that offer our models. Before deploying a model, we evaluate its capabilities and risks, train it to follow safety requirements, and test whether its safeguards hold up when people deliberately try to bypass them. As we describe in our approach to safety and alignment, we combine safeguards designed to reinforce one another. After deployment, we monitor for potential abuse and investigate concerns. To mitigate cyber misuse, for example, we train models to refuse harmful requests and use systems that look for suspicious patterns across interactions to decide how to respond. Trusted access programs provide another layer of protection and set eligibility requirements and conditions for access to our most powerful capabilities. Some safeguards are built into the model and others depend on the systems and people around it. Both need to be effective whether people access our models directly or through a partner. Developers and businesses should be able to choose where they access our models, with consistent safeguards across those services. We developed policies to align our safeguards across providers and are working with each of our partners to ensure their implementation meets or exceeds our safety standards. These policies apply whether people access our models directly through OpenAI, partners that host them, or through reseller partners. These policies require partners that provide access to OpenAI models to maintain safeguards consistent with our own, investigate potential violations, and take appropriate action when concerns are identified. That includes coordinating on enforcement so that restrictions remain effective across services providing access to our models. Putting this into practice means accounting for how different services work and how customers use them. Our work with customers and partners on Private Safety Processing is one example of how we can develop effective safeguards while giving customers greater choice and control over their sensitive data. We’re also updating our Usage Policies, effective November 20, 2026, to clarify the rules for safe model development and sensitive uses of AI. The updated Usage Policies build on that work by requiring services that provide direct access to our models such as model routers or AI gateways to get our review and approval before offering that access. We’ll keep explaining what’s allowed, what’s restricted, and how customers and partners can ask questions or resolve compliance concerns. As our models become more capable, we’ll keep improving how we detect, investigate, and respond to misuse. Customers can face misuse through their end users, compromised accounts, or leaked API keys and we work with them to understand and address those problems. We’re also working with customers to introduce SafetyIDs, which customers can provide to help us distinguish between individual end users in an investigation without OpenAI learning those users’ identities. With SafetyIDs, we can respond to potential misuse more precisely while reducing disruption to others. We base enforcement decisions on documented conduct and risk, apply our rules consistently, and respond in proportion to the circumstances. When we restrict access, we revisit those restrictions if meaningful changes in conduct, commitments, or safeguards address the concerns behind our decision. We want more people to benefit from AI. Clear rules and consistent safeguards should make it easier for developers and businesses to build, compete, and choose the services that work best for them.

items.title_original: NVIDIA Kumo Relational Outperforms Supervised Machine Learning on Relational Data, No Training Required

items.extracted_title: NVIDIA Kumo Relational Outperforms Supervised Machine Learning on Relational Data, No Training Required
items.extracted_excerpt: A Blog post by NVIDIA on Hugging Face
items.extracted_text_for_analysis: NVIDIA Kumo Relational Outperforms Supervised Machine Learning on Relational Data, No Training Required NVIDIA Kumo Relational is a pre-trained relational foundation model that makes predictions directly on enterprise databases. Given a predictive query, it gathers up to 10,000 historical examples as context and predicts outcomes such as churn, demand, or fraud in a single forward pass. It needs no task-specific training, no feature engineering, and no flattening of tables. Kumo Relational is the first few-shot foundation model to outperform supervised machine learning on common relational benchmarks. Across 41 tasks on 15 databases, it beats supervised relational deep learning models and expert-engineered gradient-boosted tree pipelines, and on the SAP SALT enterprise benchmark it surpasses AutoGluon ensembles by 8% in mean reciprocal rank (MRR). It scales to databases with 500B+ rows and works for humans and agents alike, through NVIDIA's open-source, GPU-native structured-data-models library or as an NVIDIA NIM. - Paper: https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.12596 - Documentation: https://docs.nvidia.com/sdgm/rfm/overview Foundation models have already rewritten the playbook for language and vision. Not long ago, production NLP meant a dedicated model per task, each fed by its own pipeline of tokenization, lemmatization, and n-grams. LLMs made that stack largely obsolete for three reasons: they were more accurate than the best task-specific models, far simpler to put into production, and flexible enough to open a new era of agentic applications. The same shift is now underway for structured data. Relational databases power the world's most critical business decisions, yet predictive modeling on them still requires weeks of feature engineering, task-specific training, and tuned pipelines. Structured data foundation models change that for the same three reasons: Better accuracy today: As drop-in replacements, these models already beat many production pipelines, especially XGBoost. On RelBench V1 classification tasks, Kumo Relational outperforms gradient-boosted trees on expert-engineered features by nearly 4 AUROC points on average. On SAP SALT, it beats XGBoost on engineered features by 7 MRR points out of the box and by 13 MRR points after fine-tuning. These results make a compelling case for replacing production XGBoost pipelines with Kumo Relational. Simplicity and agility: One pre-trained model replaces separate pipelines for individual tasks. A new prediction becomes a query instead of a project, so ML teams can finally take on use cases that traditional ML made too laborious to build at every level of the organization. Agents that can predict: LLMs let agents read, write, and reason. Structured data foundation models let them anticipate what happens next, such as which customer will churn, and act on it. Kumo Relational is already built to be called by agents, and its Predictive Query Language (PQL) gives them a simple interface for asking predictive questions. Today, we are introducing Kumo Relational (paper, documentation), a pre-trained foundation model that brings this paradigm to relational data. Connect a database, describe what to predict, and get predictions in a single forward pass. No training required. Most foundation models for structured data operate on a single flat table. Real-world data lives in relational databases instead: users connected to orders connected to products, all evolving over time. Flattening these relationships into one row through manual aggregation (e.g., "average order value in the last 30 days") loses fine-grained structural signals and takes significant human effort. Kumo Relational is a Relational Foundation Model that operates directly on the database, respecting its tables, foreign keys, and timestamps. It is pre-trained once on synthetic relational data that reflects real-world datasets and adapts to each new task through in-context learning, reading up to 10,000 context examples at inference time. Each example pairs a local subgraph around an entity at a point in time with its ground-truth target (e.g., "this user churned" or "this item sold 142 units"). ![Overview of the NVIDIA Kumo Relational system: (a) database integration, (b) a prompting interface that turns natural language into a predictive query, and (c) automatic context generation feeding the NVIDIA Kumo Relational model, which scales horizontally across tenants.] Figure 1. Overview of the Kumo Relational system. Connect a database, specify a predictive query, and Kumo Relational handles the rest, from context generation to model inference. To make a prediction, Kumo Relational has to do three things: (1) understand the values within each table, (2) relate records across tables, and (3) relate context examples with known targets to the entity being predicted. Here is how it works: ![Kumo Relational architecture: (a) context input with task, users, orders and items tables; (b) column and row attention within tables with injected context targets; (c) graph attention and cross-sample attention across tables.] Figure 2. Kumo Relational architecture: (a) context input, (b) reasoning within tables, (c) reasoning across tables. Automatic Context Generation: Tasks are written in the Predictive Query Language (PQL), a declarative interface where you state what to predict rather than how. For temporal tasks, Kumo Relational replays historical database states: it samples entity-centric subgraphs up to an anchor timestamp and computes each target from events after that timestamp, while serving the model only the data from before it. This prevents data leakage. Reasoning Within Tables: A lightweight network processes each table independently, alternating column attention (relating values within a column) and row attention (relating features within a row). The model learns which columns and rows matter for the current prediction and filters out noise before it propagates. Reasoning Across Tables: A larger network distributes the row embeddings across the relational structure via graph attention over primary-key/foreign-key relationships, interleaved with cross-sample attention across context examples. This is where relational reasoning happens, such as linking a user's profile to their transaction history. Because this stage works on row embeddings rather than on every cell in every table, the design avoids quadratic cost and scales to large contexts and deeper subgraphs. Kumo Relational is pre-trained on entirely synthetic relational data simulated to reflect real-world relational databases with diverse predictive queries. Pre-training proceeds in stages, from single tables to increasingly complex relational structures. The diverse relational databases needed for pre-training are rarely public, so synthetic data fills the gap. Kumo Relational's generator builds on the approach of PluRel (Kothapalli et al., ICML 2026), which extends single-table data generators to full relational

items.summary_en: AT&T is working with OpenAI to make legal knowledge easier to access. Learn how its LegalEdge team is rethinking intake and scaling legal judgment.
items.extracted_title: How AT&T is rethinking in-house legal work with OpenAI
items.extracted_excerpt: AT&T is working with OpenAI to make legal knowledge easier to access. Learn how its LegalEdge team is rethinking intake and scaling legal judgment.
items.extracted_text_for_analysis: AT&T’s in-house legal department has hundreds of lawyers and legal professionals around the world. Before they can advise the business, they need to assemble facts, documents, and relevant past work, often drawing on expertise held across different teams. For David McAtee, AT&T’s Senior Executive Vice President and General Counsel, making that experience easier to access is central to how the department’s work can improve. AT&T is working with OpenAI to build that next phase. “Our partnership with OpenAI is going to allow us to build that plumbing that powers the knowledge layer throughout the company and that all of us will draw into,” McAtee says. The collaboration builds on LegalEdge, AT&T’s team of attorneys, legal professionals, technologists, and project managers focused on applying AI to major legal matters. The next step is to connect more of the company’s accumulated expertise to the work arriving on a lawyer’s desk. Requests arrive from across the business, and legal teams need to respond quickly without overlooking risks. Before they can advise, they have to understand the issue, gather the relevant context and decide what needs attention first. That makes intake a critical part of protecting the business. Bill Ryan, AT&T’s Chief Compliance Officer, describes one planned initiative as an intake system with “a front door where we have natural language intake.” The system would classify and prioritize requests, connect them with relevant precedent, research, and past work, and give the responsible legal professional historical context and recommended first steps. That would give lawyers a more informed starting point, with less time spent gathering the material they need to assess a matter. Ryan sees the opportunity in helping the department bring its judgment to more of the business’s needs. “What most excites me about the future is expanding our ability to provide legal judgment at greater scale,” he says. For McAtee, the principle guiding that work remains clear: “The decision making will always remain with the lawyers.” The partnership’s goal is to put better information within reach so those lawyers can spend more time applying their expertise. Watch McAtee and Ryan discuss LegalEdge and the next phase of AT&T’s legal work with OpenAI.

items.extracted_excerpt: From local businesses to global brands, more advertisers can now reach people as they explore, compare and decide what to buy in ChatGPT.
items.extracted_text_for_analysis: ChatGPT Ads expands to 26 new countries as over 100,000 advertisers have used the platform From local businesses to global brands, more advertisers can now reach people as they explore, compare and decide what to buy in ChatGPT. More than 1.2 billion people use ChatGPT each week to explore ideas, compare options and make decisions. Ads can help people discover products and services that fit their needs, including options they might not have found otherwise. Since we launched ads just over eight months ago, over 100,000 advertisers have run campaigns on ChatGPT. Today, we’re expanding ChatGPT Ads to 26 additional countries, extending availability to 89 countries worldwide. This launch builds on our recent expansions across Europe and Southeast Asia and Taiwan. Advertising helps support free and low-cost access to ChatGPT for people around the world. Our mission is to ensure that artificial general intelligence benefits all of humanity. Ads will appear only on the Free and Go plans. Plus, Pro, and Enterprise subscriptions will remain ad-free. Following our launches in Mexico and Brazil, we’re bringing ChatGPT Ads to 14 more Latin American countries, including Argentina, Chile, Colombia, and Peru. We’re also launching in more markets across Europe, the Middle East, Africa, and Asia, including Nigeria, South Africa, Serbia, Ukraine, Cambodia, Bangladesh, and Pakistan. Advertisers can access ChatGPT Ads in these countries through technology partners or self-service access through Ads Manager(opens in a new window). In ChatGPT, people can explain what they’re looking for, ask follow-up questions, and refine their options through conversation. Someone training for their first marathon might start by exploring meal ideas for race week, then narrow their options based on their dietary preferences and how much time they have to cook. An ad relevant to that conversation could introduce them to a grocery delivery service they hadn’t considered. For local businesses, regional brands, and international companies, ChatGPT Ads gives businesses a way to introduce their products during these moments of consideration, when people are still evaluating their options and deciding what’s right for them. Protecting the trust people place in ChatGPT is foundational to our approach to advertising. Guided by OpenAI’s ads principles, we keep conversations private from advertisers and do not sell customer data. Ads in ChatGPT are clearly labeled and separate from ChatGPT’s answers, and advertising does not influence the answers ChatGPT provides. Our goal is to make ads useful to people as they pursue their goals and make decisions—and effective for the businesses that advertise with us. Our focus remains expanding access to AI while staying true to our principles. With ChatGPT Ads now available in 89 countries, our next phase of growth will include the development of additional formats, objectives, buying options, and measurement capabilities. We are also continuing to explore new ways for businesses to interact with consumers in more native ways in ChatGPT. As more people turn to ChatGPT to explore needs, evaluate options, and make decisions, we see an opportunity to help them discover products and services—and to help businesses of every size grow and thrive.

items.extracted_excerpt: OpenAI and Google Cloud are bringing frontier models and Codex workflows to Gemini’s Model Garden, available through Google Cloud Marketplace.
items.extracted_text_for_analysis: OpenAI and Google Cloud(opens in a new window) are partnering to bring OpenAI’s frontier models and Codex(opens in a new window) agentic workflows into Google Cloud’s Model Garden. The integration will give customers native access to these models to power complex agentic workflows at scale, backed by Google Cloud’s data governance and high-performance infrastructure. Google Cloud’s longstanding investment in machine learning and AI has made it a destination for AI workloads and the developers and data scientists building them. Bringing OpenAI models to its model garden gives these teams access to OpenAI’s frontier models within the environment where they already work, enabling enterprises to modernize their software development lifecycle, build agentic workflows, and change how people work. For organizations in regulated industries, deploying AI requires control over who can access sensitive data and how it is used. The integration will pair OpenAI’s frontier models with Google Cloud’s built-in access controls, centralized data governance, and high-performance infrastructure to support demanding enterprise workloads. Google Cloud customers will be able to purchase OpenAI frontier models via model garden, transacted through the Google Cloud Marketplace. Enterprises with Google Cloud spend commitments will be able to draw down their GCP commitments for these purchases. Additionally, OpenAI models will soon be available in Google Antigravity and the Gemini Agent, providing enterprise customers with model choice flexibility and the best model for each task. By expanding access through Google Cloud, we are giving enterprises greater choice in how they discover and use frontier models, with a path from evaluation to broader adoption. Microsoft remains OpenAI’s primary cloud partner.

items.extracted_title: Patch the Planet: global response coordination as agents uncover critical vulnerabilities
items.extracted_excerpt: Patch the Planet connects security researchers, maintainers, and incident responders to help address critical vulnerabilities across open source.
items.extracted_text_for_analysis: Over the past two months, we led a coalition of maintainers, researchers, and security providers to address critical vulnerabilities in PHP, an open-source programming language used to run websites and web applications. Calif identified a critical flaw using GPT‑5.6 Sol as part of our Patch the Planet(opens in a new window) initiative, with Wiz also independently discovering and reporting both vulnerabilities. PHP’s maintainers led the fixes and release, with our teams and partners like Wiz, Cloudflare, and others contributing research, technical support, and coordination to prepare protections ahead of disclosure. For organizations using PHP, the priority now is applying the fixes. We’re sharing a PHP version checker as a Codex skill(opens in a new window) to help operators identify potentially vulnerable PHP versions and, alongside PHP’s and their providers’ guidance, determine which updates apply. Given the severity of these flaws and PHP’s widespread use, we consider this one of the most impactful security issues in recent memory. It highlights how AI can uncover security flaws with internet-scale impact, but the same capabilities can also help attackers rapidly develop offensive tools and exploits. To our knowledge, frontier AI found these vulnerabilities before attackers did, opening a Defender’s Window for maintainers and security providers to prepare fixes and protections ahead of disclosure. To help more defenders use these capabilities, we’ve committed $1 billion in subsidized Daybreak access through Daybreak for Frontline Defenders, focused on organizations with limited security resources protecting essential services. As significant as they are, these bugs are among several significant vulnerabilities we’ve already found and are working to fix, and we expect similar findings to increase sharply in the coming months. Drawing on our experience thus far, we’re sharing a proposed approach, appropriate for the AI era, to responding to critical vulnerabilities in widely used software, and we’re asking the security community to help improve this framework. It brings together our models, security expertise, and maintainers to help turn findings into protection and build a response that can scale as AI capabilities advance. Getting a fix into use can mean adapting it for older releases, preparing provider mitigations, and updating systems across many organizations. A repeatable process helps those teams act quickly as more vulnerabilities are discovered. Through Patch the Planet, we contributed security expertise and model access to support the PHP response, and worked with maintainers and research partners to test fixes and prepare guidance. We also helped coordinate with infrastructure providers on protections for affected systems and engaged government cyber agencies to help guidance reach critical organizations. This supported the maintainer-led response and helped other defenders prepare. For some findings, researchers can work directly with the software’s maintainers to investigate the issue and develop a fix. Others need a wider response because they affect many products or because distributors and service providers need time (which may be in short supply if frontier capabilities are not too far ahead of those that are broadly available) to prepare updates and protections. In those cases, the proposed framework can help maintainers identify who needs to be involved and coordinate the work. The response can involve five stages: - Validate and fix the upstream vulnerability. The maintainer, researchers, and essential technical partners confirm the finding, assess its impact, and develop and test a fix. This process includes adversarial testing with frontier models to look for ways around the patch and related variants of the vulnerability. - Give affected organizations time to act. We propose a framework for considering which organizations need advance information to prepare protections, while maintainers decide whom to involve. We help with outreach, information-sharing agreements, and coordination between teams. A distributor might adapt a fix for an older release, a hosting provider might test a mitigation, and a security provider might prepare detection or prevention measures, including web application firewall (WAF) rules. - Coordinate with government partners to help protect critical systems. Government agencies play an essential role in coordinating a wider response and helping security guidance reach organizations responsible for critical infrastructure and other essential services. In the case of PHP, we worked, in collaboration with our partners, to engage with multiple parts of the U.S. government, including the White House’s Super Intelligence Force, the Office of the National Cyber Director (ONCD), the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA), as well as international partners to support that effort. - Prepare updates across affected products. As the fix, guidance, and disclosure plans become stable, maintainers can involve additional distributors, hosting and service providers, response teams, and operators to prepare updates and address gaps in coverage. - Once a patch is available, publish guidance and support deployment. Public guidance helps people assess their exposure, find authoritative updates or interim mitigations, and check that a fix is running. The response continues as operators deploy updates and report where they need help. The proposed framework considers an organization’s protective role, including protecting its own systems and customers, the time needed to act, and its ability to handle sensitive information. The same criteria would apply to comparable organizations, with maintainers deciding whom to involve ahead of disclosure. Each participant receives the information needed to carry out their protective work, from network logs with indicators of compromise to more sensitive working proof-of-concept exploits. Even limited details can reveal a vulnerability, so we weigh the risk of sharing them against the protection they enable. Teams following this framework would work with maintainers to give defenders time to prepare and reassess the timeline if there’s active exploitation in the wild, a leak, a revealing public patch, or increased risk to users from stalled remediation. The Patch the Planet website(opens in a new window) brings together public disclosures and guidance to help operators identify affected systems, find the right update, and verify that the updated software is running properly. For PHP, it points to the maintainers’ official patch and upgrade instructions and our partners’ technical research. The guidance also covers interim mitigations, when to involve a provider or expert, and backup and recovery. items.summary_en: Learn how OpenAI built ChatGPT’s LLM-powered ad stack to understand conversational intent, keep ads separate from answers, and deliver relevant ads at scale.
items.extracted_title: How we built ChatGPT’s novel ad stack for user trust and relevance
items.extracted_excerpt: Learn how OpenAI built ChatGPT’s LLM-powered ad stack to understand conversational intent, keep ads separate from answers, and deliver relevant ads at scale.
items.extracted_text_for_analysis: Traditional advertising systems are built to respond to discrete units of user intent. A user searches for or views something online, the ads system receives those queries and page views as events, and the system looks for matching ads based on those events. Building an ads stack for ChatGPT was different: user intent develops across conversations and shifts over multiple turns of a conversation, sometimes without a fitting advertising moment. To support this new paradigm, we built a bespoke ads delivery system. This new type of ad stack is based on a custom, post-trained frontier LLM that makes tool calls for retrieval (identifying the top options), ranking (predicting user engagement), relevance (evaluating the usefulness of the ad), and running auctions for final ad selection and pricing. Our ads system supports the nuance of evolving user goals by making three key design decisions: 1) implementing stateful ads sessions, meaning information is remembered across turns of a conversation and across multiple conversations, 2) relying on a custom, post-trained LLM that uses a tool call architecture to interpret a conversation’s context and underlying intent, and then effectively select, rank, and deliver ads, and 3) running the ads selection process separately from ChatGPT’s answer generation, in its own service, to keep ads from influencing answers and maintain ChatGPT’s neutral voice. We use our post-trained LLM to orchestrate the entire ads flow, determining the right ad to surface at the right time based on both the user’s current turn and conversation history. While bootstrapping a self-improving ads system like this used to take years, ChatGPT Ads reached $1 billion in annualized revenue run rate less than 200 days after launch; now, more than 100,000 advertisers have run ads on ChatGPT since launch. A conventional advertising request usually starts with a well-defined event. A user submits a search query or opens a webpage and the ads system receives a request. This type of system is fairly simple: it retrieves potential ad candidates, ranks them, runs an auction to appropriately price the opportunity, and shows the resulting ad to the user. ChatGPT does not naturally produce such a concrete moment. In a ChatGPT conversation, people arrive with goals rather than a one-answer search query. They might be planning a trip, choosing software for their business, furnishing a home, or learning a new hobby. This doesn’t all happen in one turn of a conversation. ChatGPT often helps the user clarify what matters along the way. As an example, our engineering team asked ChatGPT how to train for a race: A conversation begins with a general question about running. Several turns later, they ask about shoes to help train. The commercial meaning of the conversation changes as each constraint arrives—and this personalized context evolves across multiple sessions. A system that acted on the first message could retrieve the wrong intent entirely, potentially degrading the user’s experience and getting in their way. Building our ads system required us to move beyond the request-response advertising architecture and build an ads stack from scratch to find potential economic opportunities while prioritizing user trust and value. Turning every message into a standalone request, like a traditional ads system, would have carried a few risks in our chat use case: 1) misreading the user goal by oversimplifying it, 2) beginning the advertising flow too soon, before the user’s real need has become clear, 3) showing ads that get in the way of the user journey instead of supporting it, and 4) inefficiently rerunning the ads flow every time the request changes, creating noise and wasting cost. Instead of building around individual events, the ads system (consisting of retrieval, ranking, and delivery) maintains a stateful session, meaning the ads session runs for the duration of an eligible turn, remembering and updating information as it evolves. ChatGPT sends the initial request context to the ads server. The ads system follows and adapts to the developing exchange rather than relying on a single flattened query. The ads selection process runs alongside ChatGPT’s normal response generation to ensure the ads flow doesn’t influence ChatGPT’s responses. Ads are filtered and selected through a separate system consuming the conversation under its own eligibility, quality, and delivery constraints. This important architectural boundary—different services that use separate models and separate code—lets core ChatGPT servers handle generating the organic response; meanwhile, the ads system independently evaluates whether there’s an appropriate advertising opportunity and, if so, prepares a sponsored placement through a separate serving process. Beyond protecting the user experience, this separation has some practical consequences. ChatGPT has no dependency on the ads system—the services are in no way intertwined and don’t share a content generation model. So if the ads serving system is unavailable or slow, ChatGPT’s organic response continues unaffected. This means the ads system can’t take down or delay the ChatGPT product. The other benefit of this separation is that it keeps the bar very high for valuable ads. Returning no ad is an ordinary, successful outcome. The system only delivers an ad if it’s clearly beneficial to users and advertisers. The other key architectural component in our ads stack is the post-trained LLM that interprets conversations and runs the entire ads flow in an agentic loop—making tool calls to the core functions of the ads system, from the retrieval stage to ranking to auction and, ultimately, delivery. We call this LLM the orchestrator. The first part of an ads flow is understanding user intent to start the retrieval process, which is a fast and deliberately broad sourcing of potential ads to later filter through. Receiving the conversation incrementally creates a richer but more ambiguous retrieval problem because the ads system needs to distinguish current intent from stale context. The orchestrator must interpret references to earlier messages, recognize when a user is speaking hypothetically, and avoid treating every mention of a product or service as a request to buy something. The ads orchestrator uses the available conversation and user context, iterating to find good ads and repeatedly choosing when to call which tool with the underlying goal of finding the most appropriate ad (the ad that balances high user value and high advertiser value) for that conversation and context. If the user chooses to personalize ads, the orchestrator also considers available nonsensitive information about the user’s past conversations to find the best ad matches. items.extracted_text_for_analysis: Using thousands of AI agents to uncover new leads in biological data How OpenAI, PerturbAI, and Scripps Research used distributed AI agents to help scientists identify promising research leads in data from millions of brain cells What if scientists could uncover new clues about Alzheimer’s and Parkinson’s in minutes instead of months? Working together, OpenAI, PerturbAI(opens in a new window), and Scripps Research(opens in a new window) used thousands of AI agents powered by GPT‑Rosalind(opens in a new window) to analyze and interpret existing experimental data from millions of mouse brain cells(opens in a new window) in just 32 minutes. The agents connected the effects of gene disruptions with findings from scientific literature, uncovering unexpected biological connections that can help scientists understand disease and identify research directions for new treatments. The work shows how AI can help researchers explore more of what large biological experiments reveal. Modern experiments generate far more data than scientists can thoroughly investigate. Researchers can now alter thousands of genes and measure their effects across millions of cells. But understanding what these results mean for human disease requires connecting complex experimental findings with decades of scattered scientific knowledge. This is where AI can help scientists uncover promising leads that might otherwise be missed. “We build cell atlases so that other scientists can make discoveries we haven’t imagined yet. AI could help more researchers explore these resources and turn unexpected observations into new questions to test.” The team divided the analysis among thousands of AI agents powered by GPT‑Rosalind, an approach we call distributed biological reasoning. The agents examined a whole-brain CRISPR atlas(opens in a new window), a dataset showing how gene disruptions affect different types of cells across the mouse brain. Each agent investigated a gene disruption, analyzed cellular responses, searched scientific literature, and proposed explanations for the results. Their reports were combined into a reasoning atlas linking genes, cellular effects, relevant publications, and possible biological mechanisms. The research team estimated that comparable human analysis and literature review, conducted one perturbation at a time, would take months to a year. The agents reproduced findings from human analyses while uncovering additional leads. Their assessments of novelty and scientific value also aligned with judgments from blinded human experts. These findings help prioritize further experiments needed to test the proposed biological mechanisms. Some of these insights point to new leads for understanding brain disease. The agents identified unexpected differences in how two disease-linked genes affect brain cells differently, as well as a potential connection between cholesterol regulation and neurodegeneration. These findings could help scientists investigate how disease develops and where future treatments might intervene. “Sometimes the clues are already there, scattered across different fields—we just haven’t connected them. The possible link between neuronal function and cholesterol metabolism shows how those pieces, once brought together, can give us a new way to think about disease biology.” Researchers can begin exploring these findings today. The reasoning atlas is available(opens in a new window), allowing scientists to compare related genes, investigate unexpected responses, and identify promising leads to pursue. New discoveries often emerge when researchers from different fields bring their expertise together and connect familiar ideas in unexpected ways. AI can significantly scale these connections by linking new data with knowledge scattered across disciplines. The opportunity goes beyond analyzing data faster. By combining AI with experimental biology, human expertise, and scientific literature, we can help scientists turn more of their data into testable ideas. Some of an experiment’s most interesting clues lie outside the story scientists set out to investigate. In a dataset spanning thousands of perturbations, those clues can be easy to miss. The agents identified an unexpected difference between Tsc1 and Tsc2, two genes that work together to control mTOR, a major regulator of cell growth, metabolism, and aging. Disrupting either gene had similar effects in several groups of neurons. But in the cerebellum, which helps coordinate movement, Tsc2 disruption altered the activity of dozens of genes involved in neuronal communication, while Tsc1 disruption produced little change. That difference may be relevant to human disease. In people with tuberous sclerosis, abnormalities in the cerebellum are strongly linked to TSC2 mutations. While medicines that reduce mTOR activity can treat certain brain tumors and seizures, learning and behavioral difficulties associated with the disease remain challenging to address. The agents pinpointed a specific group of neurons and cellular changes worth investigating: which changes might existing medicines correct, and which might point to new treatment approaches? This gives researchers a more specific set of questions to test in the lab. Could a single agent given the entire dataset do just as well as thousands of agents working in parallel? We tested this while keeping the model and resources fixed. As the workload grew, the single agent searched less of the literature, citing only 11 references at the largest workload, while the distributed agents cited more than 700 references. Human experts also preferred the distributed-agent interpretations. Scientists have limited time and often focus on the strongest signals in their data. Distributed agents can help examine a wider range of responses, including subtle or unexpected ones, and connect them with relevant scientific literature. Running the agents in parallel allows many perturbations to be investigated at once. This helps scientists explore more of what an experiment contains and identify promising leads that might otherwise be missed. A finding becomes more valuable when it points to an experiment worth doing. The agents found one such lead in DCTN1, a gene whose mutations cause Perry syndrome, a neurodegenerative disease with Parkinson-like symptoms. DCTN1 is involved in moving cargo inside neurons. In the whole-brain CRISPR atlas, disrupting Dctn1 increased the expression of genes involved in making cholesterol. The agents connected this observation with research suggesting that problems with cholesterol transport may cause cells to make more cholesterol. This raised a question for follow-up experiments: could DCTN1 disruption change how cholesterol is distributed within neurons, and could those changes contribute to neurodegeneration?
